text: Raw alert volume — how many alerts fired today — tells you almost nothing by itself. The useful version breaks that number down at least three ways: by shift or day so a spike is visible against a normal baseline, by severity so a day with a few high-severity alerts isn't judged the same as a day with hundreds of low-severity ones, and by source, because one specific rule or feed is often driving most of the total.

Alert volume describes what came in. Workload metrics describe what it cost the humans handling it: alerts closed per analyst per shift, and the average time spent triaging one alert. A rising alerts-per-analyst number paired with a shrinking time-per-alert usually means analysts are rushing, not that triage got easier. A growing backlog carried into the next shift is the same signal from a different angle.

Put volume and workload together and a real problem becomes visible that neither number shows alone. Say alert volume has held steady near 400 per shift for months, but alerts per analyst has climbed from 50 to 80 because two analysts left and weren't replaced, and time per alert has dropped from six minutes to under three.

Read separately, neither change looks alarming. Read together, they describe analysts under-resourced for the volume they're receiving, moving faster than careful triage allows — exactly the condition under which a real attack gets waved through as a false positive instead of caught.

These numbers exist to surface three specific problems before they cause a missed incident: a source generating disproportionate low-value volume is a candidate for rule tuning; a backlog or per-analyst workload that keeps climbing is a numeric case for more headcount, not just a feeling that the team is stretched; and analysts sustained at a high alerts-per-shift rate for weeks are at real risk of alert fatigue — rubber-stamping alerts as false just to keep the queue moving.
